title: "When a network pays off"
description: "A network pays off when the response carries more signal than noise and the inputs matter in combinations nobody has named. On the survey's noisy counts it trails a random forest; on a water-mass band in temperature and salinity, two hidden units beat every other model."
order: 4

---

#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
f2 <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- \(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)

{{< new-terms >}}

## Two things decide whether a network pays off

"Neural networks need a lot of data" is common advice, but it does not say how much, and
marine surveys usually have hundreds of rows, not millions. This page fits a network
beside simpler models on two problems of that size. On the survey's counts it loses; on a
water mass it wins clearly. The number of rows does not explain the difference. Two
things do.

The first is how much of the response is signal. Each count is the number expected at
that station plus [noise](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd), the part no
model can predict, and [The bias–variance trade-off](../05-generalisation/bias-variance.qmd)
showed that on this survey the noise is the largest part of the error. A network has many
weights, and on noisy data they fit the noise as readily as the signal.

The second is whether what matters is a combination of the inputs. Oceanographers meet
this on the **T–S diagram**, which plots temperature against salinity. A water mass shows
up on it as a diagonal band, because what identifies the water is how temperature and
salinity go together, not a threshold on either one.

The three kinds of model the course has fitted draw such a boundary in different ways. A
linear model such as logistic regression adds up its weighted inputs, so its boundary is
one straight line: it can say which side of the line a point lies, but not that it lies
between two lines. A decision tree splits on one input at a time, so every edge it draws
is horizontal or vertical, and a diagonal edge becomes a staircase. A hidden unit takes a
weighted sum of all its inputs before it bends ([Neurons, layers and
activations](what-a-network-is.qmd)), so its bend runs along a tilted line. Two opposing
bends leave a band between them, just as two bends made a hump in temperature on that page.

::: {.diagram}
![Drawing a diagonal band: a linear model draws one straight line, a decision tree a staircase of rectangles, and a network two tilted bends with the band between them.](img/diagonal-band.svg){fig-alt="Three cards, each a scatter of temperature against salinity in which the filled points lie in a diagonal band and the open points lie outside it. Linear model, one straight line: a single blue line runs along the lower edge of the band and everything above it is shaded, open points included; one weighted sum of the inputs draws one straight boundary, and it cannot fence in a band. Decision tree, one input at a time: six orange rectangles step up along the band, covering it with some open points inside the steps; each split cuts one input, so a diagonal edge becomes steps, and smoothing the steps takes rows. Network, tilted bends: two parallel green lines labelled unit 1 and unit 2 run along the two edges of the band, with the band shaded between them; each hidden unit bends along a tilted line and two make a band, and the weights find the tilt."}
:::

## Worked example

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

Three models predict abundance from eight inputs: depth, temperature, chlorophyll,
salinity, substrate, season, longitude and latitude. They are linear regression, the
random forest from [Random forests and
boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) and the network that `mlp()`
fitted on [Training a network](training-a-network.qmd), with eight hidden units and a
small penalty. A quarter of the sites are held back as test sites, split by site as on
[Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |>
  select(station_id, site_id, abundance, depth_m, temperature_c,
         chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season,
         longitude, latitude) |>
  drop_na()

set.seed(99)
split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
  salinity_psu + substrate + season + longitude + latitude

count_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

models <- list(
  `Linear regression` = linear_reg(),
  `Random forest`     = rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
    set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |>
    set_mode("regression"),
  `Neural network`    = mlp(hidden_units = 8, penalty = 0.01, epochs = 500) |>
    set_engine("nnet") |>
    set_mode("regression")
)

fit_all <- function(recipe) {
  map(models, \(model) {
    set.seed(1)
    fit(workflow(recipe, model), train)
  })
}

count_fits <- fit_all(count_recipe)
predicted <- map(count_fits, \(fitted) predict(fitted, test)$.pred)

scores <- tibble(
  Model = names(models),
  `Test RMSE` = map_dbl(predicted, \(p) rmse_vec(test$abundance, p))
)
scores |> mutate(`Test RMSE` = round(`Test RMSE`, 2))
```

```{r}
#| label: count-numbers
#| include: false
on_counts <- set_names(scores$`Test RMSE`, scores$Model)
baseline <- rmse_vec(test$abundance, rep(mean(train$abundance), nrow(test)))
n_inputs <- ncol(bake(prep(count_recipe), new_data = NULL)) - 1
n_weights <- (n_inputs + 1) * 8 + 9
```

`step_zv()` drops any column with the same value in every row, which a 0/1 column for a
rare substrate can be in a small sample. The models train on `r nrow(train)` stations and
are scored on `r nrow(test)`.

### The network is short of signal, not of rows

Predicting the mean count of the training stations at every test station gives an RMSE of
`r f2(baseline)` individuals. The random forest beats that at `r f2(on_counts["Random forest"])`,
and linear regression at `r f2(on_counts["Linear regression"])`. The network, with
`r n_weights` weights, scores `r f2(on_counts["Neural network"])`: last of the three, and
only `r f2(baseline - on_counts["Neural network"])` better than predicting the mean.

That alone does not say whether the network needs more stations or less noise. The survey
is simulated, so each station's [true mean
count](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd), the number the
simulation drew its count around, is known. It is a check only: no real survey has this
column. The three fits are scored against it, and then the three models are trained again
on the same stations with the true mean count as the response, which removes the noise
and keeps everything else.

```{r}
#| label: true-means
check_data <- load_coastal_survey_truth()
train <- left_join(train, check_data, by = "station_id")
test  <- left_join(test, check_data, by = "station_id")

mean_recipe <- recipe(update(predictors, true_mean ~ .), data = train) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

mean_fits <- fit_all(mean_recipe)

checked <- tibble(
  Model = names(models),
  `Trained on counts` = map_dbl(predicted, \(p) rmse_vec(test$true_mean, p)),
  `Trained on true means` = map_dbl(mean_fits, \(fitted)
    rmse_vec(test$true_mean, predict(fitted, test)$.pred))
)
checked |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

```{r}
#| label: check-numbers
#| include: false
from_counts <- set_names(checked$`Trained on counts`, checked$Model)
from_means <- set_names(checked$`Trained on true means`, checked$Model)
gain <- round(100 * (1 - from_means["Neural network"] /
                       from_means["Linear regression"]))
```

The table gives each model's RMSE against the true mean counts at the test stations.
Trained on the counts, the network is still last, at `r f2(from_counts["Neural network"])`
against `r f2(from_counts["Random forest"])` for the forest: its weights followed the
noise in the training counts. Trained on the true means of the same stations, it comes
first at `r f2(from_means["Neural network"])`, against
`r f2(from_means["Random forest"])` for the forest and
`r f2(from_means["Linear regression"])` for linear regression, `r gain`% better than
linear regression. A straight line cannot follow the humped responses in the survey; the
network can.

Nothing changed but the noise. The same `r nrow(train)` stations were enough for the
network to learn the response once the noise was gone, so it was short of signal, not of
rows. A smaller network or a larger penalty, chosen by cross-validation as on
[Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd), would
follow less of the noise, and would end up close to linear regression.

### Two hidden units draw the diagonal band

The coastal survey has no water mass, so one is simulated. Salinity rises with temperature
across the stations, and a station belongs to the water-mass core when its T–S point falls
inside a narrow diagonal band. Four models are fitted with their usual settings: logistic
regression, a decision tree, a 500-tree random forest and a network with two hidden units,
one for each edge of the band.

```{r}
#| label: water-mass
make_water_mass <- function(n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  temperature_c <- runif(n, 2, 16)
  salinity_psu  <- 33.0 + 0.10 * temperature_c + rnorm(n, 0, 0.45)
  in_core <- abs(salinity_psu - 33.0 - 0.16 * temperature_c + 0.32) < 0.30
  tibble(temperature_c, salinity_psu,
         water_mass = factor(if_else(in_core, "core", "outside"),
                             levels = c("core", "outside")))
}

water_train <- make_water_mass(200, seed = 1)
water_test  <- make_water_mass(2000, seed = 2)

water_recipe <- recipe(water_mass ~ temperature_c + salinity_psu,
                       data = water_train) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

classifiers <- list(
  `Logistic regression` = logistic_reg(),
  `Decision tree`  = decision_tree(tree_depth = 8, min_n = 5) |>
    set_mode("classification"),
  `Random forest`  = rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
    set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |>
    set_mode("classification"),
  `Neural network` = mlp(hidden_units = 2, penalty = 0.001, epochs = 800) |>
    set_engine("nnet") |>
    set_mode("classification")
)

water_fits <- map(classifiers, \(spec) {
  set.seed(5)
  fit(workflow(water_recipe, spec), water_train)
})

water_scores <- imap_dfr(water_fits, \(fitted, model) {
  scored <- augment(fitted, water_test)
  tibble(Model = model,
         `Test ROC AUC` = roc_auc_vec(water_test$water_mass, scored$.pred_core),
         `Test accuracy` = accuracy_vec(water_test$water_mass, scored$.pred_class))
})
water_scores |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: water-numbers
#| include: false
auc <- set_names(water_scores$`Test ROC AUC`, water_scores$Model)
band_weights <- length(extract_fit_engine(water_fits$`Neural network`)$wts)
```

`r nrow(water_train)` stations train the models and
`r format(nrow(water_test), big.mark = ",")` test them;
`r round(100 * mean(water_train$water_mass == "core"))`% of the training stations are in
the core. Only two inputs are involved, and the band's edges are straight: the task is
not hard, it is just not lined up with either input. The ROC AUC, from [Classification
performance measures](../07-validation/classification-metrics.qmd), scores how well a
model ranks core stations above the rest, from 0.5 for guessing to 1 for a perfect
ranking. Logistic regression reaches `r f3(auc["Logistic regression"])`, the decision
tree `r f3(auc["Decision tree"])` and the random forest `r f3(auc["Random forest"])`. The
network, with `r band_weights` weights, reaches `r f3(auc["Neural network"])`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-boundaries
#| fig-cap: "What each model predicts over the whole temperature–salinity plane, fitted to the 200 training stations shown as points. Logistic regression draws one straight line, the tree and the forest draw steps, and the network draws the band."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels of temperature on the horizontal axis against salinity on the vertical, each shaded by the predicted class, core or outside, with the training stations drawn as filled points for core and crosses for outside. The core stations form a narrow diagonal band rising from low temperature and salinity to high. Logistic regression shades one side of a single straight line as core, a wedge that includes much of the plane outside the band. The decision tree shades a few large rectangles along the band and a strip across the top at high salinity. The random forest shades a band with ragged, stepped edges along the core stations, widening into a block across the top right at high salinity. The neural network shades a clean straight-edged diagonal band along the core stations."
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 7.2
plane <- expand_grid(
  temperature_c = seq(2, 16, length.out = 220),
  salinity_psu  = seq(min(water_train$salinity_psu), max(water_train$salinity_psu),
                      length.out = 220)
)

panels <- imap(water_fits, \(fitted, model) {
  plane |>
    mutate(predicted = predict(fitted, plane)$.pred_class) |>
    ggplot(aes(temperature_c, salinity_psu)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = predicted), alpha = 0.45) +
    geom_point(data = water_train, aes(shape = water_mass), size = 1.3) +
    scale_fill_ml(labels = str_to_sentence) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(core = 16, outside = 4),
                       labels = str_to_sentence) +
    labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Salinity (PSU)", subtitle = model,
         fill = "Predicted", shape = "Station")
})

wrap_plots(panels, nrow = 2) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

The panels show the diagram's three boundaries on real fits. Logistic regression can only
call one side of its line core. The tree covers the band with a few large rectangles, and
the forest, averaging 500 trees, with many small steps that still leave ragged edges. The
network's two hidden units sit along the band's two edges.

A staircase gets closer to a diagonal as the steps get smaller, and smaller steps need more
stations. Each model is refitted on new training sets of three sizes and scored on the same
test stations.

```{r}
#| label: sizes
by_size <- map_dfr(c(100, 400, 1600), \(n) {
  training <- make_water_mass(n, seed = 10 + n)
  imap_dfr(classifiers, \(spec, model) {
    set.seed(5)
    fitted <- fit(workflow(water_recipe, spec), training)
    tibble(`Training stations` = n, model,
           auc = roc_auc_vec(water_test$water_mass,
                             augment(fitted, water_test)$.pred_core))
  })
})

by_size |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = auc) |>
  mutate(across(-`Training stations`, \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: size-numbers
#| include: false
at_size <- \(n, m) f3(by_size$auc[by_size$`Training stations` == n &
                                    by_size$model == m])
```

The network reaches `r at_size(100, "Neural network")` with only 100 training stations.
The forest climbs from `r at_size(100, "Random forest")` to
`r at_size(1600, "Random forest")` as its steps shrink, and needs 1,600 stations to come
close. Logistic regression stays near `r at_size(1600, "Logistic regression")` at every
size: more stations cannot give it a second line.

### Feature engineering lets logistic regression match the network

An oceanographer who knows the slope of the band on the T–S diagram can hand that
combination to a simpler model as a new column. Building inputs from domain knowledge like
this is called **feature engineering**. A band is a range of the combination, so the
recipe adds its square too (`step_poly()`, as in [Linear and polynomial
regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd)).

```{r}
#| label: named-combination
named_recipe <- recipe(water_mass ~ temperature_c + salinity_psu,
                       data = water_train) |>
  step_mutate(combination = salinity_psu - 0.16 * temperature_c) |>
  step_rm(temperature_c, salinity_psu) |>
  step_normalize(combination) |>
  step_poly(combination, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE))

# Run on its own, glm() warns here: the combination separates the two
# classes completely.
named_fit <- fit(workflow(named_recipe, logistic_reg()), water_train)
named_auc <- roc_auc_vec(water_test$water_mass,
                         augment(named_fit, water_test)$.pred_core)
round(named_auc, 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: named-numbers
#| include: false
n_coefficients <- c("one", "two", "three", "four")[nrow(tidy(named_fit))]
```

Run on its own, `glm()` warns that the fit did not converge and that some fitted
probabilities are 0 or 1. The combination separates core from outside completely, which
[Finding the
parameters](../04-how-algorithms-learn/parameter-estimation.qmd#separation-leaves-no-lowest-point)
calls separation: the coefficients grow without limit, but the ranking is right. With the
named combination, logistic regression reaches a ROC AUC of `r f3(named_auc)` with
`r n_coefficients` coefficients, level with the network.

When you can name the combination, feature engineering beats a network: fewer
coefficients, and each one can be read. A network's value is that it finds combinations
for you when you cannot name them. That value grows with the number of inputs, because the
number of possible combinations grows with them.

## Look for signal and combinations nobody can name

The same property explains why networks lead on images and sound. A single pixel means
little; an edge is a combination of neighbouring pixels, and a fish is a combination of
edges. Nobody can list those combinations, and there are millions of candidates.

**A network is worth trying when:**

- The inputs are raw and many, such as imagery, spectra, acoustic echoes or DNA sequences,
  and the useful features are combinations nobody can list. Much marine imaging work starts
  from a network already trained on millions of general images and retrains it on a few
  hundred of its own (**transfer learning**), which needs far fewer labelled examples.
- The response carries more signal than noise, such as a well-calibrated sensor reading
  rather than a single count. You cannot compute true mean counts for real data, but you
  can estimate the noise from duplicate tows, replicate grabs, or two observers counting
  the same sample.

**A forest or a simpler model is the better start when:**

- The data are a table of a few hundred rows of ecological covariates with a noisy
  response, as on the coastal survey, where the random forest led.
- You can name the combination that matters. Add it as a column, and a model whose
  coefficients can be read will do as well.
- You need to report effects or repeat a result exactly. A network's weights mean little
  one by one, and its random start changes the result between runs; [Feature
  importance](../10-interpretation/feature-importance.qmd) works on its predictions
  instead.

Real water masses are curved and overlap, and there a forest closes much of the gap; the
straight band makes the mechanism easy to see. The networks in this section have one small
hidden layer. The networks behind marine image analysis are far larger, but they win for
the same reason.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The maths, if you want it

A hidden unit computes $h = g(w_1 T + w_2 S + b)$ from temperature $T$ and salinity $S$.
It takes the same value everywhere along a line $w_1 T + w_2 S = c$, so its bend runs
across the plane along a tilted line whose slope is set by $w_1$ and $w_2$. A network with
two hidden units predicts $\sigma(v_1 h_1 + v_2 h_2 + b_0)$. If both units share the same
tilt, with their bends at two different values of $c$ and $v_1$, $v_2$ of opposite sign,
the sum is high only between the two lines: a band. A tree's split $T < t$ or $S < s$ is
the special case $w_2 = 0$ or $w_1 = 0$, which is why it can only cut along the axes.
:::

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- A network pays off when the response carries more signal than noise and the inputs
  matter in combinations nobody has named. The number of rows alone does not decide it.
- On the survey's counts the network scored `r f2(on_counts["Neural network"])`, behind
  the forest's `r f2(on_counts["Random forest"])`. Trained on the true mean counts of the
  same stations, it came first: it was short of signal, not of rows.
- A hidden unit bends along a tilted line, so two of them fence in a water mass's band
  on a **T–S diagram**: a ROC AUC of `r f3(auc["Neural network"])` from
  `r nrow(water_train)` stations, where the forest reached `r f3(auc["Random forest"])`.
- If you can name the combination, add it as a column (**feature engineering**):
  logistic regression then matches the network.
- Start with a forest for a few hundred rows of noisy ecological covariates; try a
  network, often through **transfer learning**, for raw, many-input data such as images,
  spectra and sound.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Replace `abundance` with the presence column `present` and RMSE with `roc_auc`, using
   `set_mode("classification")` and `logistic_reg()` in place of linear regression.
   Presence carries less noise than the count: does the network get closer to the forest?
2. Set `hidden_units = 1` in the water-mass network. What can one tilted bend draw, and
   how does its ROC AUC compare with logistic regression's?
3. Curve the band: in `make_water_mass()`, replace `0.16 * temperature_c` with a quadratic
   in temperature and refit all four models. Does the network keep its lead, and does the
   forest close the gap?
